newsitem.title: UK: Oil traders warm to OPEC freeze, wary of spring thaw.
newsitem.headline: Oil traders warm to OPEC freeze, wary of spring thaw.

text.p: World oil markets gave a cautious nod of approval on Thursday to OPEC's widely anticipated deal to freeze oil output until the middle of next year.
But leading oil traders, while welcoming the deal, warned that prices may begin to sink in the spring when seasonally weak demand begins to undermine the market.

The price of Brent crude, the world benchmark, was trading 16 cents a barrel higher at $22.88 on London's International Petroleum Exchange immediately after the deal was struck at the meeting of OPEC ministers in Vienna.

This is some way below the post-Gulf War high of $25.06 hit last month but well above $17.14, the price a year ago. Crude prices have been climbing in the last three years from a low of under $13.00, fuelling inflation fears in oil-thirsty Western nations.

Oil traders said the pact to keep the OPEC output ceiling at 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd) would underpin winter oil markets and offset any downward pressure on prices from a resumption of Iraqi exports.
"OPEC are getting much better at taking the temperature of the market," said Bob Finch, the head of trading at Vitol SA, the world's biggest independent oil trading and refining company.

Earlier this week Iraq and the United Nations reached agreement on an "oil-for-food" deal that will allow Baghdad to resume selling oil, possibly in December, for the first time since the 1990 Gulf crisis.
"The Iraqi news helped nudge them (OPEC) towards the inevitable rollover but despite that, they look like a more confident organisation than they did a few years ago," said Finch.

Oil traders said an early resumption of Iraqi exports could easily be absorbed by thirsty winter markets which are struggling to rebuild historically low stocks. But the seasonally weak second quarter will be vulnerable to price falls, particularly on crude, they said.

"Winter weather is always important for demand but it could be critical this year because of the low stocks," Finch said. On the supply side he saw OPEC discipline, the flow rates of oil from Iraq and selling by other oil producers as important.

Iraqi crude exports are likely to average around 500,000 to 550,000 bpd during the first 180 days or six months, assuming current prices and that 85 percent of the oil heads west and 15 percent east. Under the deal with the U.N., Iraq can export oil until a cash ceiling of $2 billion is hit.
If this is front-loaded to allow a bigger volume in the first quarter than the second, any downward pressure on prices is likely to be minimised, oil traders said.

"Supply towards the end of the first quarter is going to be a big factor to watch. But the market will naturally tend to take more Iraqi oil in the first quarter," said Finch. A key factor would be whether the "oil-for-food" deal was extended, he added.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) in Paris expects the call on OPEC oil to be 26.5 million bpd in the first quarter of 1997, compared to OPEC output of less than 26.0 million in recent months. This should allow room for most of the Iraqi oil.

But over the past two years the IEA has seen the call on OPEC oil fall dramatically between the first and second quarters. The IEA reported a drop of 2.5 million bpd in 1995 and 4.2 million this year.

"OPEC did a pretty decent job this time. They couldn't be expected to do much more given all the imponderables in the market," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil trading division at Bankers Trust International in London.

He noted the potential for some weakness in the second quarter but added, "Maybe the second quarter will be a period to re-stocking. It worries me slightly what stocks will be at the end of the first quarter".
Typically world oil markets eat into oil stocks during the winter months as a buffer against rising demand.
But fading demand in the spring, together with a rise in production from North Sea fields towards the end of the first quarter may be enough to tip prices lower by late spring.
Scott Carter, senior oil trader at Tosco Petroleum in London, saw the second quarter as a potentially weak period for crude.
"OPEC will keep the market bouyant for the next three or four months but the second quarter looks much less certain," he said.
"Crude has the potential to fall quite sharply, depending on how quickly demand falls away in the spring.
"But in Europe at least some oil products have the potential to stay reasonably strong and keep refinery margins pretty healthy."
The Brent crude market already reflects those expectations of a weaker second quarter. Physical Brent crude for the first quarter was pegged around $21.80 a barrel compared to $20.25 for the second.
But oil products are holding up reasonably well compared to Brent.

Gasoline, typically strong in the spring as oil companies stock up ahead of the summer driving seaon, has just emerged from a price dip in Europe and is trading just $5.10 a barrel above Brent in the second quarter next year.
This is well below an average of nearly $6.00 above in the same period this year but many oil dealers expect the gasoline premium above Brent to firm as spring appraoches.
Gas oil, which is usually weak in the spring, is buoyant. The second quarter next year is $4.60 a barrel over Brent compared to an average $3.60 premium in the first quarter this year.
"The pressure looks like it will be felt on crude rather than products," said Carter.
